title: Genesis 1:9–13
context: Day three gathers the waters so dry land appears, then fills that land with vegetation according to kinds. Verses 9–13 give Earth and Seas their names, pronounce the land good, and let the earth sprout seed-bearing plants and fruit trees—still before the sun is mentioned. Habitable earth and fruitfulness come by the same creating word.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Dry land, seas, and the earth made fruitful: older Arminian and Reformed writers, each in their own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: The third day's work is related in these verses; the forming the sea and the dry land, and making the earth fruitful. Hitherto the power of the Creator had been employed about the upper part of the visible world; now he descends to this lower world, designed for the children of men, both for their habitation, and their maintenance. How the earth was prepared to be a habitation for man by the gathering of the waters together, and making the dry land appear.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Gen 1:9)

reformed.quote: Let the earth bring forth grass Hitherto the earth was naked and barren, now the Lord fructifies it by his word. For though it was already destined to bring forth fruit, yet till new virtue proceeded from the mouth of God, it must remain dry and empty. For neither was it naturally fit to produce anything, nor had it a germinating principle from any other source, till the mouth of the Lord was opened.

verses.text: God said, “Let the waters under the sky be gathered together to one place, and let the dry land appear;” and it was so.
verses.arminianNotes:
God said, “Let the waters under the sky be gathered… and let the dry land appear.” And it was so. Habitable earth arrives by command, a stage prepared for plants, animals, and finally image-bearers.

Wesleyan Arminians hear provision before inhabitants. God freely makes a home; the gathering of waters is kindness, not a reluctant concession to chaos.
verses.reformedNotes:
Waters gather to one place and dry land appears because God said so. The sea’s bounds are His.

We dwell on dry ground by command. The elements do not graciously recede on their own; paternal government holds the waters so that a world may be inhabited.

verses.text: God called the dry land “earth”, and the gathering together of the waters he called “seas”. God saw that it was good.
verses.arminianNotes:
God called dry land Earth and the gathered waters Seas, and saw that it was good. Names and a verdict: the split world is not a mistake.

Earth and Seas are gifts with names, judged good before anyone farms or sails. Gratitude is the fitting first theology of geography.
verses.reformedNotes:
Naming Earth and Seas is further lordship; “good” is God’s own stamp on the arrangement of dry ground and gathered water.

Comfort: the world’s map is not self-made. What God names and approves stands under His care—seas gathered, land given—so creaturely life will have a place.

verses.text: God said, “Let the earth yield grass, herbs yielding seeds, and fruit trees bearing fruit after their kind, with their seeds in it, on the earth;” and it was so.
verses.arminianNotes:
God said, “Let the earth yield grass… each according to its kind.” Seed and fruit are in the plants from the start; kinds are His idea, not later human sorting only.

Arminians affirm both the earth’s fruitfulness and its dependence. The soil brings forth because God enables it; kinds are a generous stability, not a prison.
verses.reformedNotes:
The barren earth is told to sprout, with seed according to kind. Fruitfulness is word-given before sun or farmer.

The earth had no germinating principle until God opened His mouth. What we now call nature’s law is the lingering force of that once-spoken command.

verses.text: The earth yielded grass, herbs yielding seed after their kind, and trees bearing fruit, with their seeds in it, after their kind; and God saw that it was good.
verses.arminianNotes:
The earth actually brought forth vegetation according to kinds, and God saw that it was good. Command becomes harvest; kinds hold.

Secondary causes are no illusion—the earth brought forth—under the God who spoke. Creaturely agency is not a threat to the Creator; it is His intended means.
verses.reformedNotes:
The earth brought forth as ordered: plants and trees according to their kinds, and God judged it good.

Kinds are stable because God made them so. The earth’s obedience displays effectual speech; what He specified, the ground produced, and He called that yield good.

verses.text: There was evening and there was morning, a third day.
verses.arminianNotes:
Land, seas, and a green world now stand, still waiting for lights, animals, and humankind.

Classical Arminians receive the day’s close as God’s pacing of gifts. The week is not rushed; fruitfulness is in place before those who will eat it exist.
verses.reformedNotes:
The third day ends as the first two did—by God’s marking of evening and morning. Land and green life now sit inside a counted day.

Time remains His. The vegetated earth sits inside a week God counts, a reminder that history and harvest unfold on His schedule, not on an independent clock.
